findings.title: Local cache is filled before the DB write, letting devices bypass the limit on retry
findings.body: In tagDeviceUI the device's cache key is written with `a.localCache.SetDefault(key, struct{}{})` *before* `CreateOrUpdateDevice` is called. This PR now propagates the DB error out of TagDevice (the added `return err` at the end of TagDevice) and client.go turns `anonstore.ErrDeviceLimitReached` into an authentication failure. So when a brand-new device is rejected because the limit is reached, its cache key is already populated for 29 minutes. The next request from that same device hits the cache, tagDeviceUI returns nil, TagDevice returns nil, and authentication succeeds even though the limit is still reached and the device was never persisted. In practice the device limit can be defeated by simply retrying/refreshing. Transient DB errors have the same effect (no retry for 29 minutes). Populate the cache only after CreateOrUpdateDevice succeeds, or delete the key on error.

findings.title: Provider signatures changed without updating callers/generated DI, breaking the build
findings.body: `ProvideAnonDBStore` now requires an extra `deviceLimit int64` argument and `ProvideAnonymousDeviceService` (impl.go) changed its third parameter from `anonstore.AnonStore` to `db.DB`. Both are dependency-injection providers whose call sites live outside the changed files (the wire provider set / generated `wire_gen.go`). Those callers still invoke the old signatures (passing an `AnonStore` where `db.DB` is now expected, and calling `ProvideAnonDBStore(sqlStore)` with one arg), so the package will not compile. The generated/registered providers must be regenerated/updated in this PR; wire cannot synthesize the bare `int64` argument either.

findings.title: Device-limit check is a non-atomic count-then-insert
findings.body: CreateOrUpdateDevice runs `CountDevices` in one DB session and then performs the INSERT/UPDATE in a separate session with no transaction or locking. Under concurrent anonymous traffic, two (or more) new devices can both observe `count < s.deviceLimit` and both insert, so the configured cap can be exceeded by up to the degree of concurrency. Enforce the limit atomically (single transaction with row locking, or an atomic conditional insert) if the cap is meant to be hard.

findings.title: Device tagging moved onto the synchronous authentication hot path
findings.body: Tagging used to run in a fire-and-forget goroutine with a 2-minute background timeout, so DB writes never affected request latency. It is now a synchronous call in Authenticate using the request context. Every cache-miss request (once per device per ~29 min, and always when the limit check runs it also issues a COUNT plus INSERT) now blocks authentication on DB round trips, adds latency to anonymous requests, and lets a slow or cancelled request context silently drop the tag. Consider keeping the write off the auth path or bounding it with a timeout/background context.

findings.title: Frontend type says `number | undefined` but server always sends a number
findings.body: The Go DTO field is `int64` without `omitempty`, so `anonymousDeviceLimit` is always present in the frontend settings (0 when unset), and GrafanaBootConfig's default of `undefined` is overwritten by 0. The TS declaration `number | undefined` therefore can never be undefined at runtime. Consumers cannot distinguish "not configured" from an explicit 0, and any `!== undefined` check will treat the disabled default as a real limit of 0. Either emit it as `omitempty`/pointer on the server and keep `undefined` in TS, or type it as `number` and document that 0 means "no limit".

findings.title: New `[auth.anonymous] device_limit` option is not documented in the sample config
findings.body: The new `device_limit` key is read in `readAuthSettings` but is not added to `conf/sample.ini`/`conf/defaults.ini` (or the docs). Operators have no way to discover the option or its default (0 = disabled). Add the documented default to the sample config and reference documentation.

findings.title: New test only covers rejecting new devices, not allowing existing ones at the limit
findings.body: TestIntegrationBeyondDeviceLimit only asserts that a second, new device gets ErrDeviceLimitReached. It does not exercise the other required behavior: when the limit is reached, an already-tracked device must still be allowed to refresh via the updateDevice path. That branch contains non-trivial `updated_at BETWEEN ... AND ...` window logic, and a regression there (e.g., legitimately active devices being wrongly rejected) would not be caught. Add a test that re-tags the existing device after the limit is reached and expects success.
